pr_title: net: lwm2m: rework error handing in content formaters
pr_body:
This PR introduces a set of changes to improve error detection in content encoders/decoders;
* Modify the encoders/decoders generic API, to return `ssize_t` instead of `size_t`, therefore allowing to report error conditions (typically -ENOMEM for encoders when we run out of memory in a packer, or -ENODATA for decoders when there is no expected data in received packet),
* Align all of the existing encoders/decoders with the API changes, adding additional error checks where appropriate,
* Add a set of unit tests for each content type encoder/decoder,
* And finally fix a couple of minor bug detected by the aforementioned tests.

Fixes #41996.
pr_comments:
> * Modify the encoders/decoders generic API, to return `ssize_t` instead of `size_t`, therefore allowing to report error conditions (typically -ENOMEM for encoders when we run out of memory in a packer, or -ENODATA for decoders when there is no expected data in received packet),

Posix defines that ssize_t can have a value -1 so strictly speaking any other <0 value would not be returnable. Not sure if this is a big issue here as the APIs we are defining here are not POSIX but still.
https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/ssize_t.3.html
https://jameshfisher.com/2017/02/22/ssize_t/

So if we want to use ssize_t like POSIX defines, then we would only be able to return -1 and set errno to the desired error value. This sounds/feels also quite cumbersome to me.

Just pondering here that would it make sense to use normal int value to tell error (<0), and 0 as success and then have a separate size_t value returned as a parameter, what do you think?

Some discussion in PR https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/27165
Posix doc at https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/sys_types.h.html

> I think we could use the `int` for the return value, I just wonder do we really need that extra parameter for returning the size written? Those functions work with datagrams, which size is limited to 64K so in theory there's no way we'll overflow `int` if we return the number of bytes written/read directly through the return value (we could use `int32_t` just to be 100% sure).

In that case, we could just return int as it can handle all the values returned.
@jukkar I've updated the APIs to use `int` instead. Additionally added a couple of commits addressing nits found by the CI.
@carlescufi Any chance to get this in before code freeze?
@petterssonandreas Thank you for the feedback, I've addressed your comments.
This PR fixes #41996, so merging it in the 3.0.0 window.

issue_context.title: LWM2M writing too long strings trigger post_write_cb with previously written value
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
You get no error or warning if you try to write a too long string from a LWM2M server, instead the code will silently use the last written value (that had a good length), and trigger post_write_cb and the like with that value, effectily making it look like you wrote the same value once again.

**To Reproduce**
We can define an IPSO object with a field of type String, and set its resource to some static char array, and using the size of that array as the size of the resource. We can also register eg. post_write callback for this field.

If we then write that field from a LWM2M server with a string that is longer than the resource array, we don't get an error. Instead, the resource array is simply not overwritten with the new value, but keeps the old value, and then carries on processing the write as if that value is the newly written value. This will then trigger eg. post_write callback with the previous value, making it look like we write the same value again.

**Expected behavior**
I would expect the lwm2m engine to throw an error if the string is too long, not allowing the write, and stopping the processing of it.

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/875c75c4f9f75927cec94c580d16d42eb5d26c0e/subsys/net/lib/lwm2m/lwm2m_rw_oma_tlv.c#L632-L634

The above code has a TODO regarding this, and does return 0, indicating that nothing was written. But lwm2m engine does not take this into account:

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/f2ca6a8c22052eac8f10cdda41d477716f85eb02/subsys/net/lib/lwm2m/lwm2m_engine.c#L2555-L2558

ignoring the return from the engine_get_string, and just assuming the `write_buf` was written to.

This would be easy to fix, changing the code above to:

```c
case LWM2M_RES_TYPE_STRING:
	if (engine_get_string(&msg->in, write_buf, write_buf_len) <= 0) {
		/* -EEXIST will generate Bad Request LWM2M response. */
		return -EEXIST;
	}
	len = strlen((char *)write_buf);
	break;
```

Using either `== 0` or `<= 0` depending on what we want to cover.

**Impact**
I have found no other way to actually check and error on the length of a string. I have tried adding a longer validate buffer, and that works in some sense, but basically only delaying the problem, since the exakt same problem will occur when the written string is longer than the validate buffer.

I can design other guards for this, or adding more fields for the length etc, but it's not pretty or clean. I can also design my code to not care about the multiple writes of the same value, but the problem is really that the user of the server thinks that the new, too long, value was actually written.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: Linux (Ubuntu 20.04)
 - Toolchain: gnuarmemb
 - Zephyr version: Tested on tag `v2.7.0-ncs1`, but also check Zephyr main and saw no fix to this.
 - LWM2M server: Eclipse Leshan, but with our own modifications
comments:
Hi @petterssonandreas, thanks for the report.

I think this issue should already be fixed in my PR (https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/41744), where I've reworked error handling in the LwM2M content writers in general. Could you have a look?

Hi @rlubos,

Great that you have made a PR for this! I took a quick look, and left some comments. I am not too familiar with the code so didn't really look at everything, but I tried to look at the parts that this issue covers.

And yes, I think this is mostly covered by your PR, although some of my comments point out code that could be potentially harmful (or at least still annoying to users), the ones where we read/write the write_buf without checking the return code.

review_comments:
Are we trying to be too clever here.
For example, if someone tries to read whole firmware object, and we would try to dump the whole firmware binary into message, it is OK to run out of memory as it is too big to handle. However, we might still have enough memory for rest of the resources.

Allowing to continue when `ENOMEM` is reported would require further rework fo the content writers - TLV or JSON will insert appropriate metadata in the packet first (TLV header, JSON tokens). If we fail to write the payload afterward, we still end up with a malformed packed (it should be required from content writers to undo any changes done to the packet). Therefore for now I've decided to treat `ENOMEM` as fatal.

Another thing is whether handling the requests partially is ok - responding with an error message could hint the server that it should query each resource individually, otherwise the event would go unnoticed, resulting in outdated reasource values on the server side.

Isn't this potentially bad? If `engine_get_string` produced an error, which we now can see by checking `ret`, we have no idea what `write_buf` actually contains right? Of course, this is only a read, but it could potentially read indefinitely, right, since we have no way of knowing that the string is terminated?
I prefer this early return, because that makes it clear what we do for errors. But we don't use early return in the other get functions, so maybe convert all to early returns?
I've updated other functions to return early as well, instead of nesting code within if.
For TLV there's never a case where there is no data (i. e. 0 is returned) - either there is at least TLV header (and thus the return value is positive), or an error code is returned.
This seems bad, do we really want to write the data to `write_buf` without checking `ret` first to make sure we didn't get any errors? Similarly for all the other types.
You're right, this isn't right to write the value in case of error, I've added additional error check before write here and in other cases.
